28294f9dfd40589f1a343f6fd8a7f9decf0e88ac.subject: Cover every chunk-world.yml dispatch input in the Chunker Actions UI
28294f9dfd40589f1a343f6fd8a7f9decf0e88ac.body:
The GitHub Actions panel only ever sent target-format and a config blob; the
other seven workflow_dispatch inputs (world-source, world, world-repository,
prune-bounds, output-name, output, max-jobs, regions-per-shard) were silently
hard-coded in ipc.ts, so a user could never point the workflow at an existing
release asset or artifact, bound its region-planning trim, name its output, ask
for a release alongside the artifact, or tune its job/shard sizing.

ChunkerActionsPanel.vue now offers a real, validated, localized control for
every one of the ten inputs; ipc.ts validates and forwards them, skipping this
app's own upload when world-source/world point at something that already
exists, and remembers the exact dispatched output-name so collection still
finds the right archive inside the artifact regardless of what name was typed.

A new hand-written guard (scripts/check-chunker-ui-inventory.mjs, run through
workflowUiInventory.test.ts) fails when a workflow input has no matching UI
literal and dispatch literal, or the UI names an input the workflow dropped;
verified red by deleting one inventory row and green after restoring it.

ae00618d1285581214d285bf8e50c23570c1e8a7.subject: Fix three integration-tip defects: hosted classification, workflow drift, packaging split
ae00618d1285581214d285bf8e50c23570c1e8a7.body:
capabilityProfile.ts never classified chunkerActions:*, so a hosted deployment
would have refused it by pure accident of nobody writing a line down. It gets
the same opt-in github shape as its close cousin cirender -- both upload a
world/config and dispatch a GitHub Actions run, so both need the same
credential and the same honesty about needing it.

chunk-world.yml's target-format input was still free-text months after the
app's own picker grew a real 18-format enum, so a typo dispatched happily and
failed a workflow run minutes later instead of failing the dropdown instantly.
It is now a type: choice with the app's own list, byte-for-byte, so
check-workflow-drift.mjs actually has something to compare.

The packaging config had quietly grown chunk-world.yml onto the SAME
extraResources filter that CI_WORKFLOW_FILE_NAMES governs -- which sounds like
tidying up and is actually a landmine: bootstrapCiRepository() writes every
file on that list into a repository the instant somebody sets up cloud map
rendering, credentials and all, no Chunker involved. Folding a Chunker workflow
into that list would have quietly installed a world-conversion pipeline nobody
asked for onto every render bootstrap. It gets its own resources/chunk-workflow
destination instead, and chunkeractions/ipc.ts now reads from there.

capabilityProfile.ts 一直冇幫 chunkerActions:* 做分類，托管環境會因為冇人寫低
決定而預設拒絕，而唔係因為諗清楚先拒絕。而家同佢個表親 cirender 用返同一套
github opt-in 邏輯，兩個都係上傳嘢再叫 GitHub Actions 走一轉，理應要求同一個
憑證。chunk-world.yml 個 target-format 輸入仲用緊自由文字，人哋 app 個揀單
早就有齊 18 個格式，打錯字唔會即刻話你知，要等個 workflow 行到一半先炸。而家
改做 choice，同 app 個列表一字不差。打包設定仲靜雞雞將 chunk-world.yml 塞咗入
cirender 專用嗰個檔案清單度 -- 呢個唔係執靚啲，係地雷：一開部署渲染機就會將
成個轉換 workflow 唔問自取咁裝落去，跟埋憑證。而家分返開兩個目的地。

400fc2844941e887ee379f7da782ad595ffc9f53.subject: Real M3 card group anatomy for Settings, plus a genuine narrow-window Clipping found and fixed
400fc2844941e887ee379f7da782ad595ffc9f53.body:
The first pass at this only bumped padding numbers, which the coordinator
correctly called a tweak rather than the asked-for Material Design 3 revamp.
SettingsSection.vue's card is now built from the real M3 token layer
instead of hand-picked pixel values: title-medium/body-medium typescale
for the header, surface-container for the card fill, outline-variant for
the divider between stacked cards, and a new exported .mb-setting__row
list-item utility (56px minimum, leading-icon/content/trailing grid, a
state layer drawn from the M3 hover/pressed opacity tokens) for any card
whose body is a stack of simple rows. The settings search-match list in
AppSettings.vue now uses that same row anatomy instead of its own
hand-rolled hover tint. The docked-left vertical tab strip with
aria-orientation and the anchored regex-searchable search field were
already correctly implemented and needed no rework.

Every individual settings row in this dialog (theme picker, size dial,
download concurrency, Java runtime, storage) genuinely needs multi-line
supporting text, hints and provenance lines per this project's own
settings-explanation rules, so forcing them into rigid single-line 56px
rows would have fought that requirement rather than served it - they stay
full-width M3 card content, which is itself a legitimate M3 pattern, and
that trade-off is recorded honestly rather than papered over with a
row wrapper that does not fit what it wraps.

then `pnpm -r build`) and drove the real Electron app through the cheap
Lowlevel headless route end to end: real onboarding clicks, real Settings
open, real CDP-driven viewport and theme/language changes. That surfaced
a genuine defect no source read would have caught: at a 320px window,
the tab strip's fixed 10rem minimum width left the detail pane so little
room that its new title-medium heading broke every character of "Mojang
download consent" onto its own line. Fixed with a narrow-width floor and
re-captured the same tuple to confirm real word-wrapping. Verified clean
at 320px and normal desktop width, English and bilingual, dark and light.

Added a source-level regression pinning that narrow-width floor (watched
it fail against the old 10rem value, then pass), a card-anatomy test for
the new token-drawn padding/gap/divider, and a check that Settings never
opts the strip out of its default vertical placement. Updated the token
name one earlier test still asserted after the surface-container/
outline-variant tokens replaced the hand-mixed rgba tint. Documented the
new layout in docs/display-and-ease-of-use.md, the closest existing
article to AppSettings.vue's own display section - no dedicated
Settings-dialog article existed to update.

check-webapp-parity.mjs stayed green throughout, including a full
BlueMap-Material submodule checkout so it actually inspects all four
surfaces instead of skipping silently.

1b63fd348bf852a6fe3950ade8e1c425a4075dfd.subject: Fix regex-builder popover crash, sweep clipped card titles, revamp Settings card spacing
1b63fd348bf852a6fe3950ade8e1c425a4075dfd.body:
Refs #175: opening the settings search field's regex builder could crash
the renderer in a packaged build. ConfigRegexBuilder is v-menu popover
content Vuetify repositions with a ResizeObserver on every resize; a
max-height/overflow-y:auto card whose text sits near that cap is the
textbook setup for a scrollbar-toggle layout loop (scrollbar width changes
the content box, which reflows wrapped text past/under the cap, which
toggles the scrollbar again, forever) - and Vuetify's own flip-loop guard
only watches for an alternating boolean, not a plain width oscillation, so
nothing there catches it. scrollbar-gutter: stable reserves the track
unconditionally and removes the toggle. Applied the same defensive fix to
the two other anchored, scrollable popovers with the identical shape
(TabGroupPicker, TabStrip). Added a regression test that mounts the field,
clicks the affordance, and asserts the popover actually renders instead of
hanging.

Clipping sweep: sixteen more v-card-title elements across the config,
project, remote and mounts screens were still sitting on Vuetify's default
overflow:hidden/white-space:nowrap/text-overflow:ellipsis, the exact
truncation this codebase had already fixed once in
DependencyInstallerPanel.vue - a translated title long enough for
bilingual mode or Cantonese was silently clipped with no ellipsis painted.
Fixed all sixteen with the same white-space:normal/overflow-wrap:anywhere
pattern, routed around v-dialog/v-menu teleport boundaries where present.
Audited every other capped/scrollable overlay in settings, tabs and config
for a missing overflow-y:auto (none found - the rest of this app already
gets that right).

Settings dialog: .mb-setting shipped at 16px padding / 12px gap, which is
exactly what "a bit cramped" describes for a Material Design 3 card. Bumped to the
M3 24px/16px card anatomy and added a token-drawn divider between stacked
sections. Tab strip docking, vertical aria-orientation and search-wired
regex builders were already implemented correctly in TabStrip/
TabbedNavigation and needed no change. Two new source-level tests pin the
padding/gap numbers and the divider rule so a later edit cannot quietly
revert them.

check-webapp-parity.mjs verified green with the BlueMap submodule actually
checked out (was silently skipping the whole check before).

cccade075ead063984351a1b6075bea246ce11b1.subject: Record the preserved primary-checkout work, without taking it
cccade075ead063984351a1b6075bea246ce11b1.body:
Merged with the ours strategy, deliberately, and that choice is the whole content of this
commit so it is worth being explicit about.

The preserved branch holds what the primary Worktree was carrying uncommitted: a
describe-jars change naming the fork as the source repository, and a submodule pointer at
a3b2d9eb. Both are already here and both are already better. The describe-jars fix is
identical except for four lines of comment, where this branch's wording says CI staged the
jar and then refused it and main's says CI built it correctly and then refused to stage it -
main describes the failure in the right order. The submodule here is 7e7cfd03, which is
newer than a3b2d9eb and contains it.

So an ordinary merge would take a worse comment and an older submodule, which is a
regression dressed as integration. Ours keeps main's content and still makes the preserved
commit an ancestor, so the history survives permanently in this repository's own graph and
the branch can be retired without losing the record.

The comparison that justifies this was run rather than assumed: the two files were read and
diffed byte for byte, and the submodule ancestry was checked, before anything was merged.

325e18a311aeb17cfbb85b13b938ce113c16be10.subject: Run the purity guard from the suite, and prove it both ways
325e18a311aeb17cfbb85b13b938ce113c16be10.body:
It was an npm script, which means it ran when somebody remembered. GitHub Actions runs no
tests and gates nothing here, so a check living only in CI would never run at all and one
living only in a script runs about as often. A guard nobody runs is decoration, and this
one guards drift that is invisible by nature: a hardcoded colour renders perfectly, it is
simply the one thing on the page ignoring the reader's theme.

Four tests, and two of them are the pair that matters. One writes an undeclared colour where
the guard actually looks and asserts it is refused by name; the other writes the same colour
with a declaration and asserts it is accepted. Without the second, a guard that refused
everything would pass the first, and an exemption route that had quietly stopped working
would make the guard unusable rather than strict. The probe is removed in a finally, so a
failure cannot leave the tree dirty.

Writing them found a real hole in the guard. Its skip patterns used a character class
meaning 'either separator', that class lost a backslash on its way through tooling, and the
survivor matched only forward slashes - so on Windows the generated-theme directory was
never skipped at all and the seed colour every role is derived from was reported as a
violation. Paths are normalised to forward slashes before matching now, so a pattern never
has to know about separators.

聲明咗就一定綠。

be35fac8b85f1cd5132b06ee5091661701edea70.subject: Commit the world-backup record into the repository, not only onto releases
be35fac8b85f1cd5132b06ee5091661701edea70.body:
Rendering already leaves a backup behind: the world is packed, split and published
as release assets with a Cheap LFS pointer and a backup.json sidecar, on a release
nothing in this codebase can delete or overwrite.

What was missing is any record of it in the repository. catalog.ts answers 'what
backups exist' by listing releases over the network every time, so the answer needs
a connection, a credential that can still see the repository, and GitHub being up.
Clone the repository and you have no idea what is in it - a strange property for a
backup, since the thing you reach for when something has gone wrong is the thing
that only exists while everything is working.

So the pointer is committed too. A pointer is a few hundred bytes naming the
release, the asset, the size and the hash; it is designed to stand in for the large
binary, which is exactly what a committed record needs to be. git clone now brings
the map of every world backup with it.

The bytes written are the uploader's, passed through unaltered, and a caller that
supplies anything else is refused - the format is a shipped contract shared with a
sibling application and its own module says not to invent near-misses of it.
Everything this project wants to say about a backup goes in the index beside it,
for the same reason the sidecar exists.

The commit is optimistic and the conflict is expected. Appending means two renders
finishing together race, and the loser would otherwise overwrite the winner with an
index that never knew about it - the worst outcome for a record whose whole job is
not to lose things. It re-reads and retries on the typed conflict, a bounded number
of times, and a failure never fails the render: the world is already durable by
then, and trading that for a missing convenience would be a bad bargain.

7de6d9e1ae1bebce249bb991a609660d8d6c948e.subject: Make the workflows follow the app instead of restating where it lives
7de6d9e1ae1bebce249bb991a609660d8d6c948e.body:
The workflows are full of facts about this repository that they cannot check.
design/packages/app appears as a literal string a dozen times in ci.yml alone.
node-version: 22 is copied into all eight workflows while the real constraint
lives in engines.node. The product name is duplicated out of the packaging config
by hand. None of it is wrong today; all of it goes wrong silently the moment
somebody moves a package or bumps a runtime, and the first thing that notices is
a red run minutes into CI, a long way from the change that caused it.

workflow-manifest.mjs discovers those facts rather than restating them. Packages
are found by the name in their own package.json, walking the pnpm workspace
globs, so renaming a directory changes nothing and renaming a package fails
loudly - which is the right way round. The Node major comes from engines.node.
The product name, artifact name and the three managed workflow file names come
from electron-builder.config.cjs, which is required rather than parsed: its module
body only touches CSC_* variables and exports a static literal, and a regex parse
would have to re-implement string escaping and would miss the day one of those
values is computed. The env mutation is snapshotted and restored, so importing it
into a test worker cannot leak it.

check-workflow-drift.mjs compares what the workflows say against what the manifest
finds, and reports each disagreement as a file, a line and the edit that fixes it.
Its inventory of checked facts is hand-written on purpose: a rule that only
checked the paths it happened to find would pass just as cleanly on a workflow
that had stopped mentioning the app at all.

It runs locally, deliberately. GitHub Actions runs no tests and gates nothing here,
so a check living only in CI would never run; one living only in an npm script
would run only when somebody remembered. workflowDrift.test.ts spawns it from the
suite - spawns rather than imports, because scripts/ is outside design/ and Vite's
server.fs.allow refuses the import in a way that reads as a resolution failure
rather than a boundary.

Proven by breaking it. Moving design/packages/app to design/packages/desktop-shell
turns the check red with 13 named disagreements and exit 1, and turns the vitest
gate red too; moving it back returns both to green with no tracked change. Bumping
engines.node to 24 catches all 16 stale node-version pins the same way.

e00bcd2c541b683163a06979db5906458bd3e1f8.subject: Say when this build was made, and refuse to guess when it does not know
e00bcd2c541b683163a06979db5906458bd3e1f8.body:
About printed a version and stopped there, which is half an answer: two builds a week
apart can carry the same version string whenever a release cadence pauses, and the
version alone cannot tell them apart. So the page now states when this exact build was
made, in the reader's own timezone, to the second, with the zone named.

Where the instant comes from matters more than that it appears. It is frozen into the
bundle by esbuild at build time, from the committer date of the exact commit being
built, and it is deterministic: two builds of one commit agree, and anybody can check it
with `git show`. What it is emphatically not is `new Date()` at run time, which is the
launch time of a binary that may have sat on a disk for a month and would render as a
confident fact that is simply false. There is deliberately no such fallback anywhere in
this path, and a comment beside the resolver says so, because that single line is the
whole difference between provenance and decoration and it is the line somebody will be
tempted to add the first time they meet an unavailable state.

Three states, kept distinct rather than collapsed into two: a recorded instant, an
honest "build time not recorded" for a source export with no git history to read, and
silence when the shell is simply too old to have been asked. The third is not the second.

Two defects found by looking at what actually rendered rather than at the code:

`Intl.DateTimeFormat` refuses to combine `dateStyle`/`timeStyle` with `timeZoneName` and
throws. Written the tidy way, the catch below swallowed that throw on every single call
and rendered a raw ISO string instead of local time, which reads as a deliberate format
rather than a branch that never once succeeded. Now built from component options, and
asserted on the rendered output rather than on the intent.

And this file's own test suite had all thirteen tests failing before any of this, on
`[Vuetify] Could not find defaults instance`, because the page renders real Vuetify
components while the test never installed the plugin its neighbours install. Repaired,
so the five new cases actually run rather than joining a file nobody could have noticed
was red. All 18 pass. The negative one is the one that matters: a build with no recorded
time must never show the current year.

Verified in the built bundle, not just in the tests: the main bundle carries
`builtAt: "2026-08-25T05:04:33.000Z"`, which is exactly HEAD's committer date.

2c2769ccda9a6ad07f9e7c8e1ccdbf405b99c6be.subject: Give adoption the candidate browser its button always implied
2c2769ccda9a6ad07f9e7c8e1ccdbf405b99c6be.body:
Clicking "Adopt an existing container" could do nothing at all, and the design
prototype had already written that down as a known gap: "Adoption is built, but
the button is not wired ... Clicking it today opens nothing and shows no error."

The whole defect was four lines in App.vue. It called adoptDiscover(), read
discovered.ok ? discovered.value?.[0] : undefined, and returned early when
that was falsy. Three failures, and every one of them looks identical from the
outside, which is why this survived so long.

It dropped the Answer's failure, so a build that has not wired the namespace, a
refused Docker permission and a machine with no containers on it were the same
event. It returned early with no dialog and no message, so a live-looking
control did nothing and said nothing. And it took index zero, so a machine with
three adoptable containers offered exactly one of them and never mentioned the
other two.

AdoptionBrowser.vue is the missing step. It owns discovery and has to answer for
every outcome: in flight, failed with the store's own sentence and a way to try
again, empty with what would be here and where it comes from, or the full list
with nothing hidden and nothing chosen on the user's behalf. Flavour and version
are guesses in the type, so they read as guesses on screen, and when neither can
be guessed it says so rather than leaving a gap. It carries its own search with
the anchored regex builder, like every other list in this application, and every
row is a real button.

It is mounted at all three sites the review dialog is mounted at, because a
shell variant with the dialog and no browser is a variant where the original
defect is still alive in one corner.

adoptionBrowser.contract.test.ts holds both halves, because the component can be
honest while the shell never asks it. It was proven red four separate ways
before this landed: the browser showing only the first candidate, the browser
swallowing the failure, the shell going back to index zero, and one shell
variant losing its browser. Each turned green again when restored.

One thing worth recording for whoever writes the next source-reading guard. The
first version of the App.vue assertion failed immediately, on the comment that
explains the fix rather than on any code, because the comment quotes the old
line. It strips comments now. A guard that cannot tell code from prose punishes
documenting the change.

Verified: 98 typecheck errors in the ui package before this change and 98 after,
the same ones. mcserver and App suites 13 failed before and 13 failed after, the
same ones, with 7 new passing tests on top. Nothing here fixes those 13; they
predate it.

cda9d25b249b6fcf60358183dcef0ed5d16865ef.subject: Replace informal house wording with plain terms and add an externally-configured wording guard
cda9d25b249b6fcf60358183dcef0ed5d16865ef.body:
The repository is public, and a set of informal internal shorthand terms had
leaked into tracked prose: comments, handoff and roadmap notes, test fixtures,
and a handful of commit messages that the generated changelog copies verbatim.
None of it changed behaviour -- it was all prose, log strings, and one code
marker (the Material Design 3 purity guard's own exemption marker, which
carried the same shorthand baked into a literal string used across twenty-odd
files) -- so every occurrence is swapped for the ordinary English word it
already stood for: a clipping defect stays a clipping defect, a guard stays a
guard, GitHub Actions stays GitHub Actions.

Renamed materialPurity.test.ts to materialPurity.test.ts and its internal
"pure-material-design"/"material-exempt:" markers to "pure-material-design"/
"material-exempt:", updating every file that declares an exemption with the
old marker and every doc that named the old filename.

The generated changelog is derived from git history, and history is immutable
here, so a handful of old commit subjects and bodies still carry the old
wording verbatim. Added scripts/changelog-overrides.json: a committed,
per-commit-SHA map of neutral subject/body text that build-changelog.mjs
consults before falling back to the raw commit message (and before the
existing full-redaction list), so the published changelog and its in-app
viewer read cleanly without rewriting a single commit. Filled it for every
commit a full-history sweep found still carrying the old wording.

check-published-text.mjs, reading its term list from a file outside this
repository named by WORLDLENS_PRIVATE_TERMS_FILE. With that variable unset --

skipped and exits 0. With it set, it scans every tracked file and fails naming
file:line for any hit, and separately reports (without failing) any of the

overrides file as the fix. Wired as `check:private-terms` in design/
package.json, documented in AGENTS.md, and covered by a vitest wrapper that
exercises the skip path (the only path a shared checkout can exercise without
holding the private term list itself).

via the environment variable, and correctly fails naming the exact file and
line when a term is deliberately reintroduced. build-changelog.mjs --check,
lint-workflows.mjs, and the site's article-bundle assertion all still pass;
the renamed and new test files pass under vitest.

7f6f4e4096b8ad3c38019a557d3e892e07a63bef.subject: Integrate the two green large-world and server-creation branches, and fix what meeting main broke
7f6f4e4096b8ad3c38019a557d3e892e07a63bef.body:
Both branches were green on their own base and reported so honestly in their handoff. Merged
onto the main that had moved under them, they were not: six type errors and one copy check.

Five of the six were one omission seen from five angles. The large-world lane added synthetic
world generation that answers through the transport failure shape, and its five new outcome
codes - a generation with no live renderer to own it, a second one started while the first
runs, the generator throwing, the destination already existing, and cancellation - were never
added to the failure union. Each lane compiled alone; neither had reason to widen a type the
other was about to depend on. The union carries them now, each documented for what it names.

The sixth was a signature: the generation contract hands its zip step a record, and the
generator's own zip function wants the record it produced, with a name and a region list. An
adapter builds the second from the first, reading the region directory, rather than widening
the contract to carry a type only one implementation needs.

The copy check is the finding worth keeping. Two keys reported "call site passes [], catalogue
has [bytes, chunks, target]" while the call site plainly passed three arguments. The scanner
finds calls by matching `t(`, `tx(` or `tp(` with nothing word-like before them, and the dialog
had aliased vue-i18n's `t` as `measuredT` - invisible to it, so only the bare-key pass saw
those keys, with nothing attached. Renamed to `tx`, which the scanner does see, and gave the
two argument-carrying calls the trailing fallback string that this codebase's convention
puts third, after the arguments - the order every other screen uses and the one the scanner
reads placeholders from.

c66cfa400545b729d5975869ec6f308da756a153.subject: Vendor Chunker, and hold it to the version the workflow downloads
c66cfa400545b729d5975869ec6f308da756a153.body:
Chunker was fetched from HiveGamesOSS' releases at run time, so it was not really
part of this build at all: an offline machine got nothing, and what a render used
was whatever that tag pointed at on the day. Vendored as a submodule, pinned to 1.10.0,
the exact tag chunk-world.yml already names. MIT, so it travels.

The claim beside it is the point of pinning. The workflow downloads a published jar
by tag and the app builds one from this source, and two different Chunkers converting
the same world is a difference nobody notices until a world comes back subtly wrong
from one route and not the other - with nothing on either side stating its version,
so it never gets diagnosed. Chunker declares no version anywhere in its source, so the
tag is the only record: the check resolves it inside the submodule and compares it with
the commit actually pinned, which needs no network. Watched it fail on 1.9.0 against
the workflow's 1.10.0, naming both commits and the line, then go green on restore.

An uninitialised submodule is skipped rather than reported. A clone without
--recurse-submodules has nothing to compare, and failing there would be a complaint
about the clone rather than about drift.

version 睇彩數。而家 vendor 咗做 submodule，釘死 1.10.0，同 workflow 講嘅一模一樣，仲加

fe4f265613bb5c19f4256c986bf910aa3fab483e.subject: A pre-publication check for internal shorthand, and one real leak it found
fe4f265613bb5c19f4256c986bf910aa3fab483e.body:
Issue #168 asked for this and named the reason: the eleven files fixed in
fa2f5abb were found by a manual sweep, and a manual sweep is exactly what will
not happen next time.

The terms are not in this repository, because holding them is the leak. The
previous sign-in guard listed seven of them in source in order to assert their
absence, which published the exact words it existed to keep unpublished. This
reads them from a file outside the repository, resolved dynamically from the
script's own location so no username, drive letter or absolute path is written
down, and skips with a printed reason and exit 0 when that file is absent. A
public repository's CI will never have it, and a check whose normal state is red
is a check everyone learns to scroll past -- which is how the workflow linter in
#167 went two weeks unread.

A hit prints as file, line and column. The term is withheld unless --show,
because printing it puts it in a terminal, a CI log or a pasted bug report, which
is the publication this exists to prevent.

It found one real leak on its first run, in docs/release-ledger.json, in a file
the manual sweep had already been over. Fixed here.

Three false-positive classes it had to learn, each one costing a wrong answer
first:

  A term found in a PNG is byte noise. Issue #168's own Verified section records
  this from the manual sweep. Skipped on a NUL byte rather than by extension, so
  an unfamiliar binary is skipped too.

  Homonyms. The memory heap, git cat-file, a Minecraft mob. 37 occurrences across
  nine hand-written files, every one reviewed by hand and recorded in an
  allowlist that holds positions and reasons and never a term. Keyed by exact
  position, so an edit that moves a line re-flags it: the review was of that
  occurrence, not of the word.

  The generated changelog and CHANGELOG.md. #168 is explicit that editing them is
  not a fix and that fixing history means a force-push. Their 67 hits are counted
  and named as accepted residue rather than failing the run.

Two of my own defects, both silent skips in the one script whose job is to miss
nothing. With no --commit-msg, commitIndex is -1, so `index !== commitIndex + 1`
is `index !== 0` and the first path argument was dropped without a word. And an
explicit directory was read as a file, threw, was swallowed by a catch, and
contributed nothing while the run still reported clean. Both found by checking a
result I did not believe.

Proven by breaking it: a new leak in a doc goes red, the same leak in a commit
message before it is written goes red, an explicitly named terms file that does
not exist skips loudly rather than quietly falling back to a different one, and
the clean tree reports no actionable hit. 11 of 11.

  pnpm published-text:check
  node scripts/check-published-text.mjs --commit-msg <file>

Refs #168

213112f86bbdb1c3cdba68a500bf8e6efc702ffb.subject: The workflow linter had drifted for two weeks, and the commit that broke it also removed the job that ran it
213112f86bbdb1c3cdba68a500bf8e6efc702ffb.body:
86024f0f deleted ci.yml's "Lint the workflow files" job under the standing policy
that GitHub Actions runs no tests and no lint. That job was the only thing that
ran scripts/lint-workflows.mjs. The same commit renamed the check job, rewrote a
step the linter fingerprints, and removed a job and a step the linter required to
exist. Nothing noticed, because the thing that would have noticed had just been
deleted. Eight ci.yml commits later it reported 12 problems and its own test
reported 6.

Every one was reviewed rather than cleared.

Action counts: 127 to 134. All seven additions are the receipt system plus a
fourth checkout, setup-node and pnpm/action-setup for render-world's receipt job.
Before moving the number I checked every one of the 134 uses across all eight
workflows against the reviewed SHA for its action: none is unpinned and none uses
a SHA the inventory had not already reviewed. PINNED_ACTIONS 6 to 10 for the four
docker actions the container-image work added, and the version resolver 2 to 3
for the image identity, which uses the committed resolver the assertion exists to
require rather than an exception to it.

Two checks removed. They required the "Check committed screenshot evidence" step
and the screenshots capture job to exist, and both went under the no-capture-gate
policy, so they asserted the presence of two things the policy forbids and failed
on every run for as long as the policy has held. Removed with about 150 lines of
mutation coverage that had been replacing text absent from the file, so each
mutation came back identical to the original and failed claiming a missing
contract. That is what the file already did for the "Verify generated changelog
is current" checks.

Two fingerprints recomputed after reading the diffs: a narrower registry token, a
manifest regenerated after the jar is staged, jar verification moved into a tested
script, and honest release-note prose about what the workflow does not run.

The condition inventory now compares as a set and names what changed. It was
order-sensitive, so swapping two jobs raised "condition inventory must match" --
which reads as an unreviewed gate appearing. Job order in YAML decides nothing;
needs: does, and execution order is covered byte-exactly by the fingerprints. It
raised false alarms, and a guard that raises false alarms is a guard nobody reads.

Then the other half of the issue: pnpm workflows:check runs the test and the
linter together, and the test now resolves every path from its own location, so
it passes from the repository root and from design/ rather than only the former.

Proven by breaking it: an unpinned tag and a new conditional gate each turn it
red, and the gate is named in the message. Restored, both green. 33 of 33.

8c718cd3df50f555ba195185c38c650e356d0a9b.subject: Reach a container's server, whether the daemon is here or in another country
8c718cd3df50f555ba195185c38c650e356d0a9b.body:
One implementation of Docker, two thin factories on top. `sshDocker.ts`
is 140 lines and none of them are the container lifecycle, because
`remote/ssh.ts` already returns a `sshCommandRunner` that IS a
`CommandRunner`. Inspecting a container on a machine across an ocean is
the same code as inspecting one here, with one substitution. That is the
seam earning its keep.

Files do not travel through the command runner, and this is the one
thing worth reading twice. `CommandOutput.stdout` is a string. Pipe a jar
or a region file through `docker cp -` and every byte that is not valid
UTF-8 comes out the other side as U+FFFD - silently, one way, looking for
all the world like a file that was always broken. So `docker cp` is
pointed at a real file on the daemon's own machine and the bytes are
moved by something that understands bytes: `fs` locally, `scp` remotely.

`docker cp` rather than `exec cat` for a reason that sounds small and is
not: it works on a STOPPED container. A bad config is the most common
reason a server will not start, so the moment somebody most needs to edit
a file is precisely the moment `exec` is unavailable.

No `--follow`, and above all no `docker attach`. An attached TTY forwards
a stray Ctrl-C straight into a live JVM, and there are people standing in
that world. The console reads the log and writes over RCON instead.

Unreachable is not stopped. There are five tests on that one distinction
alone, because "I lost the SSH connection" and "the server died" look
identical from a dropped stream, and offering a restart button for the
first one restarts a perfectly healthy server full of players.

73 tests, no daemon required.

一套 Docker 實作，兩個好薄嘅 factory。SSH 版淨係換咗個 runner - 隔住個海嗰部機，同本機一模一樣嘅 code。
檔案唔行 command runner：stdout 係 string，jar 一過就變晒 U+FFFD，仲要靜雞雞噉壞。
用 docker cp 唔用 exec cat，因為 container 停咗都用得 - 而 config 寫錯正正就係佢起唔到嗰陣。
死都唔用 docker attach：撳錯個 Ctrl-C 就連埋成個 server 一齊拉閘，入面仲有人喺度。

d56989d353c53db141a6f7ec6a046fe568c6dbee.subject: Put a map on your own domain, and out of your own house
d56989d353c53db141a6f7ec6a046fe568c6dbee.body:
Three hosting routes, one rule they share: a record that has been written is not
a site that is working. DNS propagates, a certificate gets issued, an origin has
to actually answer. Reporting "live" the moment the API call returns is the most
tempting lie in this whole feature, because the call really did succeed - and the
person opens the address thirty seconds later, gets an error, and concludes the
app is broken rather than that it is early. So applying a record reports pending,
and only an address that answers turns it live.

A record already pointing somewhere else is a conflict, not something to
overwrite. It may be serving somebody's live website, and the only sign of a
silent overwrite is their site going down. Replacing one is an explicit choice.

The proxy setting is not cosmetic either way round. A tunnel must be proxied,
because cfargotunnel.com only resolves through Cloudflare's edge - unproxied, the
record points at something the public internet cannot reach at all. Pages must
not be, because proxying in front of it before its certificate exists produces a
redirect loop that is genuinely unpleasant to diagnose.

Tunnels run in whichever of three places the person picks - the host binary, a
container on local Docker, or a container on an SSH host - and all three are argv
through the CommandRunner that dockerhosting and remote already share, which is
why all three are tested here with no daemon, no remote machine and no
cloudflared installed. None of them publishes a port: a tunnel dials outward, so
there is nothing to publish and a -p would open a hole this design does not need.
That is asserted per runtime. The image must be digest-pinned like every other
managed container, and the tunnel token goes in as an environment variable rather
than an argument so it is not sitting in docker ps for anyone on the machine.

Every surface renders a redacted command, because a preflight panel showing the
real argv puts a live credential into the next screenshot.

Two guards had to be fixed for firing on correct code, which is worth recording
because both were the same mistake: a needle too blunt for its subject. One
searched a serialised object for the token's length and hit "45" inside an ISO
timestamp; the other banned -p across a whole argv and hit ssh's own -p 22. A
guard that raises false alarms teaches people to ignore it, so both now assert what they
actually mean.

「等緊」,唔好一 call 完就話「得咗」,人哋撳落去見到 error 只會以為個
app 壞咗。已經指住第二度嗰個 record?唔郁佢,嗰個可能係人哋條命。

09c326be6e72b92d9263a5fd586128ba91e997a9.subject: Extend the import-tracking guard to catch a missing export, not just a missing file
09c326be6e72b92d9263a5fd586128ba91e997a9.body:
`importTrackingPolicy.test.ts` already fails vitest when a committed import
resolves to a file git does not track. It stayed green on commit 75f85db
anyway, because that break was a different shape wearing the same symptom:
AppearanceTarget.vue's import of releaseAppearancePopup was fine and its
target (useAppearance.ts) was fine and tracked - the file just hadn't been
given the export yet in the commit that shipped. A guard that only asks
"does this path exist in git" has nothing to say about what's written
inside a path that does.

This adds a binding-level pass beside it: for every committed import/
re-export naming a specifier, resolve the target the same way the existing
guard does (factored out as a shared resolveTarget helper), then read both
sides' COMMITTED content via one batched `git cat-file --batch` call (two
git subprocesses total, not one per import) and check the requested name
actually appears among the target's exports. `export { X as Y }` aliases,
`export *` barrels (treated as opaque - skipped rather than guessed at),
and type-only imports are exercised directly so the guard does not learn
to cry wolf. The whole file runs in ~2.5s against 1755 real source files,
git's own blob-reading being the entire cost.

Verified against the real history, not just synthetic text: run against
the actual commits, this exact detector reports both missing bindings at
75f85db and reports none at the fix commit 2f3f22e. Against the current
HEAD it is clean - that regression is already fixed - so this guard is
landing as a tripwire for the next one, not a fix for a currently-red
build.

3e2d60da4ace9f7426374c5b1eab5cd37e1d2727.subject: Extract commit links from changelog entries even when prose trails them
3e2d60da4ace9f7426374c5b1eab5cd37e1d2727.body:
The changelog parser's ENTRY regex only stripped a trailing commit link
(`- [`sha`](url)`) when nothing followed it on the line. Every "Merge pull
request" entry carries trailing prose after that link (`_(summary of N
commits, also listed here)_`), so the regex's optional group never
matched: the raw markdown stayed embedded in the subject and the site
rendered "Commit not recorded" for a commit that was, in fact, recorded.
21 of 332 entries in CHANGELOG.md were affected (one out of every sixteen
readers clicking a "why won't this link open" dead end that was never
actually dead - it just never got wired up).

Fixes the regex to capture whatever trails the commit link instead of
requiring the line to end there, and folds that trailing text back onto
the subject rather than discarding it, since "(summary of 20 commits,
also listed here)" is real information, not markup. The SHA pattern
itself is untouched - a wrong SHA is worse than no SHA, so only what is
allowed to follow the link changed, not what counts as one. Verified
against the real CHANGELOG.md: 332/332 entries now resolve a commit
(was 311/332), zero subjects retain raw link syntax, and eight recovered
SHAs were confirmed to exist via `git cat-file -e`. The in-app changelog
viewer (design/packages/ui/src/components/changelog) reads structured
data generated straight from git rather than re-parsing this markdown,
so it never had this defect. Adds four regression tests for the
merge-summary shape, generic trailing prose, leak-free subjects, and a
genuinely link-less entry.

fc084e8b8d17e86bf3c082de208f9e5d36e168b2.subject: Give the app a palette, a notice history, a changelog, and a builder on every search
fc084e8b8d17e86bf3c082de208f9e5d36e168b2.body:
Four contracts, built in parallel and wired here.

The command palette is one shortcut over every command, setting and
destination: 30 rows assembled from the registries that already exist,
so a sixth settings section or an eighth config tab appears in it on
the same commit that adds it rather than when somebody remembers. A
row that is a setting renders the real control and writes through the
same path the settings page uses; a row that is a destination says
where it goes and gets there through the shell's existing reveal, not
a second one. It defaults to the bounded card, because a search box
that swallows the window is worse than one you opted into.

The notification bell was already in the corner and was very nearly
decorative: a count over a flat list with no search and no way back.
It is a real centre now, and the contract around it stopped being an
intention: one test asserts every level lands as a corner toast with
no dialog anywhere in the document and that warnings outlive an hour
while info dismisses at five seconds, and another inventories every
dialog in the package and demands each one name the decision it asks
for. "It reports something" is not an admissible answer, and that test
caught a palette added minutes earlier.

The changelog is generated from the repository rather than written:
35 versions and 88 entries, each carrying the commit that made it,
every SHA validated before anything is written. Versions come from
tags with `rev-list --not` rather than pairwise ranges, because three
tags sit on a side branch and a range would have lost them. Categories
come from the paths a commit touched, not from its wording, because
these commits carry no feat/fix marker and a label inferred from prose
is a changelog saying what nobody wrote. CI now fails when it drifts.

The regex builder reached four collections that had no search at all -
release assets, downloads, interrupted renders and the wizard's review
lists - and the profiles list, which is the one that grows without
anybody deciding it should. That work also found the bounded-evaluation
guard was not actually bounded: the wall clock is checked between
matches, and `(a+)+$` never returns from the first one. The old
adversarial test passed because its sample was twenty characters and
the real adapter allows twenty thousand. A static guard now refuses the
two shapes that explode, and twenty-three ordinary patterns are pinned
as must-be-allowed so it cannot start raising false alarms.

cbd070779521d2647a61f335ede79bd4598d7da6.body:
The 10 GB fixture render (run wl-render-10gb-20260904) had all 30 shards go green
and then die twice at "Merge this group's shards": cancelled once, then `node`
`Killed` exit 143, a few minutes in on a standard ubuntu-24.04 runner. The planner
put every shard in one flat merge group (DEFAULT_MERGE_GROUP_SIZE=32, no memory
bound at all), and mergeShardMaps decoded EVERY shard's lod-1 lowres tiles into
~2 MB uncompressed RGBA buffers and held all of them before compositing a single
pixel. Hires tiles were never the problem - they're copied with fs.copyFile and
never touch JS memory.

Fixed both:
- merge/mergeMap.ts and resume/lowresMerge.ts now only collect lod-1 tile PATHS up
  front; a tile is decoded only when it's actually composited, so at most the
  shards sharing one lowres tile's boundary are ever decoded at once.
- resume/mergeTree.ts adds chooseMergeGroupSize(), which bounds a merge group's
  size by its shards' total tile bytes against a documented 4 GiB budget (half of
  a standard runner's ~7 GiB, leaving room for the OS/Node/checkout). This is a
  guard on top of the streaming fix, not a replacement: a group's job still
  downloads and holds every one of its shards' artifacts on disk at once.
- plan/plan.ts computes mergeGroupSize and writes it into shard-plan.json; cli.ts's
  `plan` and `waves` commands both default to plan.mergeGroupSize instead of the
  flat DEFAULT_MERGE_GROUP_SIZE, so the plan step's group-count/group-ids outputs
  and the per-merge-job `waves --group` re-derivation can never disagree. No
  workflow template changes needed - the matrix already reads group-ids from the
  plan step's outputs.

Added mergeTree.test.ts (chooseMergeGroupSize unit tests) and a plan.test.ts
describe block reproducing the 30-shard/10 GB shape; watched both go red against
the old flat sizing (temporarily reverting chooseMergeGroupSize to `return cap`)
before restoring the real implementation and confirming green. Full render-actions
suite: 288/288 passing (was 279; +9 new). Build clean. lint-workflows.mjs clean
(8 workflows). check-workflow-drift.mjs and the app's workflowTemplateSafety /
workflowTemplates / materialPurity tests show the same 3 pre-existing failures as
the unmodified integration base (verified by stashing this change and
re-running) - none touch anything this change edited.

Docs updated in docs/resumable-renders.md (English + Cantonese) with a new
subsection naming the real incident, the actual memory culprit, and how
mergeGroupSize is chosen. CHANGELOG.md is generated and was left untouched.

The world has been durable since the day uploads landed - the release assets are the
backup and nothing here makes them more so. What was missing is a record somebody can
find. Now a Cheap LFS pointer and an index are committed beside the workflows, so the
backup is discoverable by cloning rather than only by asking GitHub what releases exist.

upload.ts returns the pointer it already wrote rather than the caller re-deriving it.
Two writers of the pointer format is the one thing a restore cannot survive.

Two honest refusals rather than failures. A transport with no commit route says so once
and moves on, because that is an answer and not a problem the user can act on. A repository with no commits at all is refused with a reason, since the Git Data API cannot create
a ref in an empty one - a stack trace there would say nothing about what to do.

And it never fails the sync. The render is finished and the world is safe at that point;
turning 'the index could not be committed' into 'your render failed' would trade
something valuable for something merely nice.

The compiler caught four assumptions I had made about the transport, including that its
commit and head routes were mandatory when both are optional, and that it dealt in text
when it deals in base64. Adapted at the one place the two meet. 15 tests pass, build clean.
